title: Local Cellular INTeraction and ACTivation of Platelets in Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm
summary:
Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is a common vascular disease that, although typically asymptomatic in its early stages, is associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. Thoracic aortic aneurysm (TAA) is less common but likewise represents a serious condition with high morbidity. An aortic aneurysm is defined as a permanent dilatation of the abdominal aorta exceeding 30 mm in diameter. AAA predominantly affects older male individuals, particularly those with a history of cigarette smoking and a positive family history (Goergen et al., 2011; Leeper et al., 2011; Saatchi et al., 2012). In 2011, approximately 10,000 deaths were attributed to ruptured aortic aneurysms, corresponding to 3.2 deaths per 100,000 inhabitants (Roger et al., 2012). AAA accounts for approximately 84,000 hospital admissions annually, and around 45,000 patients undergo surgical repair each year (Roger et al., 2012; Mohan, Rozenfeld et al., 2012).
The development of aortic aneurysms is strongly influenced by established cardiovascular risk factors that are particularly prevalent in industrialized countries, including hypertension, physical inactivity, cigarette smoking, diabetes mellitus, and obesity (Lusis, 2000). In this context, the systematic evaluation of clinically relevant data obtained from archived patient records is essential for the interpretation of experimental findings and their correlation with data generated from patient-derived biological samples.
Despite considerable advances in vascular surgery and endovascular therapy, no causal pharmacological treatment is currently available for either AAA or TAA. A more comprehensive understanding of the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms is therefore essential to identify novel therapeutic targets. The proposed studies have the potential to provide important mechanistic insights into aneurysm initiation and progression and are therefore expected to have significant scientific and societal impact. An additional objective of this project is the identification of disease-specific biomarkers associated with the development and progression of AAA and TAA.
Although platelets are well recognized for their central role in haemostasis, their contribution to cardiovascular disease has gained increasing attention over the past decade. Several platelet membrane glycoproteins (GPs) have been implicated in inflammatory vascular diseases, including atherosclerosis and myocardial infarction. In contrast, the role of platelet function and platelet-mediated signalling in the pathogenesis of AAA and TAA remains largely unexplored.
conditions: Abdominal aortic aneurysm, without mention of rupture

interventions.name: Investigation of the AAA-specific pathogenic relevance of platelet activation states, erythrocyte-associated effects, and their relationship to the size and/or progression of abdominal aortic aneurysms.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Patients presenting for blood donation at the blood bank who have provided informed consent for the use of their blood samples for experimental research purposes as part of the ATLaNtA study (2018-140_2KFogU: “Potential activation mechanisms and interactions of platelets in degenerative diseases of the liver, brain, and aorta – ATLaNtA study”).
Patients with AAA/TAA fulfilling guideline-based indications for endovascular aneurysm repair (study cohort).
Patients with AAA/TAA presenting for routine follow-up examinations at the vascular outpatient clinic.
Patients with other atherosclerotic vascular diseases (excluding AAA/TAA), including peripheral arterial occlusive disease (PAOD) or carotid artery stenosis, presenting for routine follow-up examinations at the vascular outpatient clinic.
Age ≥18 years.
Technically feasible blood collection.
Written informed consent.
Exclusion criteria:
• Lack of a declaration of consent
• Psychiatric disorders and the resulting legal incapacity
• Known blood clotting disorders
• Known genetic platelet disorders
